BJT Operation and DC Bias I

Why this matters in the exam: BJT DC work is the biggest single block of the Practice Test. Q6 (load line, Q-point and β off the characteristics, 6 marks), Q7 (voltage-divider-style base network, Thévenin, DC model, and , 10 marks) and Q8 (two BJTs, 6 marks, pack E5) together are 22 of the 50 marks, and MCQs IV and V test BJT physics and the DC/AC split. The test copies workshop material closely. Q6 uses lecture-style emitter-bias characteristics, and Q7 is the same method as WS5 Q14. If you can run the two-loop method (base–emitter loop, then collector–emitter loop) without thinking, you have most of these marks.

1. The core ideas

1.1 Physics in five lines (enough for the MCQs)

  • An NPN is n (emitter, heavily doped) / p (base, thin and lightly doped) / n (collector). A PNP is the reverse. There are two junctions: emitter–base (EBJ) and collector–base (CBJ).
  • In active mode the forward-biased EBJ injects electrons into the base. The base is thin and lightly doped, so few of them recombine (about 1 %). Most of them diffuse across and are swept into the collector by the reverse-biased CBJ. Diffusion dominates at the EBJ and drift at the CBJ (Lecture 3). This is Practice Test Q1 IV, answer (a).
  • So a small controls a large , and . The base–emitter junction behaves like a diode, so it is modelled as a 0.7 V drop.
  • In an NPN, conventional current flows into the collector and base and out of the emitter. In a PNP all three directions reverse.
  • DC analysis sets the Q-point. AC analysis looks at small variations about it (Practice Test Q1 V, answer (b)).

1.2 The three modes come from the two junctions

Mode EBJ CBJ Model to draw Conditions to check
Active forward reverse V source plus a current source and V
Saturation forward forward V and V (a closed switch) , and
Cut-off reverse reverse open circuit, V

To find the mode from node voltages on an NPN, compute and . A junction is forward-biased when its p side (the base, for an NPN) is about 0.5–0.7 V above its n side. Active means and , which is the same as . For a PNP, flip every sign (, ).

Known error in the WS4 handout (Section 4). The handout lists saturation as “EBJ reverse, CBJ reverse” and cut-off as “EBJ forward, CBJ forward”. Those two rows are swapped. The table above, from the Lecture 3 slides (“Cutoff: Reverse, Reverse; Saturation: Forward, Forward”), is correct. The WS4 answer to Q6.2 (the EBJ is reverse-biased in cut-off) agrees with the lecture. Your Test 1 Reference flags the same error.

1.5 The bias configurations

The circuits all reduce to two KVL loops (Lecture 4):

Configuration Base–emitter loop Collector–emitter loop (short C–E)
Fixed bias ( from , emitter grounded)
Emitter-stabilised ( from , to ground)
Voltage divider, exact , , as above
Voltage divider, approximate (only if ) , ,
  • is “ reflected into the base”. The base loop sees the emitter resistor as times bigger, because . Lecture 4 calls it .
  • The test asks whether the resistance looking into the base, about , is large compared with . If it is, the base current hardly loads the divider and is just the unloaded divider voltage. Write the test out in every voltage-divider answer. The workshop solutions do this, and it earns marks.
  • Why emitter stabilisation is used: in the approximate method contains no β. The Q-point therefore barely moves when β changes from one transistor to the next. Pack E5 covers β sensitivity.

1.6 Load line and Q-point

The external circuit forces , which is a straight line on the – plane. The transistor must also lie on the curve for its own . The Q-point is where the two meet.

  • Cut-off end: gives .
  • Saturation end: gives . This uses the ideal ; with 0.2 V it would be , which hardly matters.
  • Increasing lowers , so the line pivots about . Lowering moves the line parallel to itself. Increasing slides Q up the line towards saturation.

Start at the New question 2 values (15 V, 3.3 kΩ, β = 100), then raise R_C and watch the line pivot about V_CC while Q slides towards saturation.

4. Traps that cost marks

  • Using without the term. In any circuit with an emitter resistor, the base loop contains , not and not . Leaving it out typically makes come out 3–5 times too big.
  • Skipping the statement. WS5 Q7 fails the test. Using the approximation there gives 16 % high. Write the test explicitly every time.
  • Mixing up and . These are equal only when the emitter is grounded. With present, . Practice Test Q7 asks for .
  • Getting wrong with present. It is , not .
  • Using the WS4 handout’s mode table. Its saturation and cut-off rows are swapped. Saturation is forward/forward and cut-off is reverse/reverse.
  • Reading “β at the Q-point” as the curve spacing. It means at that point. between neighbouring curves is , which is a different, slightly smaller number on the Q6 graph.
  • Not showing your graph readings. In Q6, write “read mA, V” before you divide. The marks are for the readings and the method.
  • Treating a negative as an arithmetic slip. It means the transistor is saturated (New question 5 shows this).

From your course files

Workshop 4: BJT physics and current bookkeeping

WS4 Q6 (course question).
6.1. Which one of the following statements is correct for a BJT transistor?
A) BJT collector current can be controlled by the voltage between The Base and emitter
B) In a PNP transistor, the Emitter is an n-type semiconductor
C) A BJT has three PN junctions that form the three terminals
D) In a PNP transistor, the Collector is an n-type semiconductor
6.2. In a PNP BJT transistor,
A) the base-emitter junction is reverse biased in the cut-off mode
B) the collector-base junction is forward biased in the cut-off mode
C) the emitter-base junction is reverse biased in the cut-off mode
D) the emitter-collector junction is reverse biased in the cut-off mode
6.3. In an NPN BJT in the active mode of operation, the Base-Emitter PN junction is forward-biased so that
A) electrons flow from base to emitter
B) holes flow from emitter to base
C) electrons flow directly from emitter to collector
D) holes flow from emitter to base

Solution
  • 6.1 (A). : the base–emitter voltage controls the collector current. A PNP has p-type emitter and collector, and a BJT has two junctions, not three.
  • 6.2 (C). In cut-off both junctions are reverse biased. Option C names the emitter-base junction. (A is the same junction written as “base-emitter”, but the official answer is C.)
  • 6.3 (D, official). The official solution reads D as “electrons flow from emitter to base”, which is the correct physics: the forward-biased B–E junction injects electrons from the n-type emitter into the base. On the question sheet, options B and D are both printed as “holes flow from emitter to base”, so D as printed is wrong for an NPN. Answer with the physics: electrons flow from emitter into the base (and only indirectly on to the collector, so C is wrong).

BJT MODES (lecture table; the WS4 handout has sat/cut-off rows swapped)
  Active: EBJ fwd, CBJ rev | VBE=0.7, IC=bIB      | check IB>0, VCE>0.2
  Sat:    EBJ fwd, CBJ fwd | VBE=0.7, VCE=0.2     | check IB,IC>0, IC<bIB
  Cutoff: both rev         | IB=IC=IE=0           | check VBE<0.7
CURRENTS  IE=IC+IB   IC=bIB   IE=(b+1)IB   IC=aIE
  a=b/(b+1)   b=a/(1-a)   ICEO=ICBO/(1-a)=(b+1)ICBO
  b_dc = ICQ/IBQ at the Q-point   (b_ac = dIC/dIB, curve spacing)
BIAS (assume active, then CHECK)
  Fixed:     IB=(VCC-0.7)/RB                 VCE=VCC-IC*RC
  Emitter:   IB=(VCC-0.7)/(RB+(b+1)RE)       VCE=VCC-IC*RC-IE*RE
  Divider exact: RTh=R1||R2, ETh=VCC*R2/(R1+R2)
                 IB=(ETh-0.7)/(RTh+(b+1)RE)
  Divider approx ONLY IF b*RE >= 10*R2  (write the test!)
                 VB=ETh, VE=VB-0.7, IC~IE=VE/RE, VCE~VCC-IC(RC+RE)
  Two supplies on the base -> superposition for VTh (PT Q7)
  Node voltages: VE=IE*RE, VC=VCC-IC*RC, VB=VE+0.7, VBC=VB-VC (<0 active)
LOAD LINE  VCE=VCC-IC(RC+RE):  (VCC,0) and (0, VCC/(RC+RE)=ICsat)
  Q = load line meets IB=IBQ curve; write the IC, VCE you read; b=ICQ/IBQ
  Design: VCC from VCE intercept, RC(+RE)=VCC/ICsat,
          RB=(VCC-0.7-IE*RE)/IBQ -> nearest standard value, quote % error
